```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE, warning=TRUE, error=FALSE, cache=FALSE,
                      fig.align="center", dpi=150, dev.args=list(pointsize=14))
# This notebook ONLY reads the saved RDS. It does not source or call a trial
# simulator, generate outcomes, fit a new design, or replace any saved data.
lyu_dir <- if(file.exists("data/table3.rds")) "." else "Lyu_2018"
saved <- readRDS(file.path(lyu_dir,"data","table3.rds"))
trials <- saved$trials
cells <- saved$cells
completed <- saved$paths
scenarios <- sort(unique(trials$scenario))
get_setting <- function(key) saved$settings$value[saved$settings$setting==key]
N <- as.integer(get_setting("maximum_patients"))
J <- as.integer(get_setting("cycles"))
target <- as.numeric(get_setting("target"))
ei <- as.numeric(strsplit(gsub("[()]","",get_setting("EI")),",")[[1]])
I <- max(saved$truth$dose)
nsim <- as.integer(get_setting("nsim_per_scenario"))
stopifnot(identical(scenarios,1:6),N==15,J==3,I==3,
          all(table(trials$scenario)==nsim),nrow(trials)==length(scenarios)*nsim,
          nrow(cells)==nrow(trials)*I*J,
          sum(cells$n)==sum(trials$patient_cycles),
          sum(cells$dlts)==sum(trials$dlts),nrow(completed)==sum(trials$n_complete))
percent <- function(x,digits=2) sprintf(paste0("%.",digits,"f%%"),100*x)
short_sequence <- function(x) gsub(",","",x,fixed=TRUE)
colors <- c(D1="#276FBF",D2="#27885E",D3="#8955B8",missing="#DDE2E6",
            correct="#D5A021",safe="#276FBF",unsafe="#CE4B4B",none="#B9C2C9")

# Reconstruct true probabilities from the SAVED run, rather than current
# simulation defaults. This keeps the analysis attached to its actual input.
truth <- lapply(scenarios,function(s) {
  a <- subset(saved$truth,scenario==s)
  a <- a[order(a$cycle,a$dose),]
  matrix(a$p,nrow=I,ncol=J)
})
names(truth) <- scenarios
true_mts <- vapply(scenarios,function(s) {
  a<-unique(trials$true_mts[trials$scenario==s]);stopifnot(length(a)==1);a
},character(1))

# All 27 fixed sequences; the design's final recommendations are nonincreasing.
doses <- as.matrix(expand.grid(rep(list(seq_len(I)),J)))
keys <- apply(doses,1,paste,collapse=",")
nonincreasing <- apply(doses,1,function(d)all(diff(d)<=0))
ordered <- order(rowSums(doses),doses[,1],doses[,2],doses[,3])
candidate_keys <- keys[ordered[nonincreasing[ordered]]]
sequence_truth <- do.call(rbind,lapply(scenarios,function(s) {
  p <- truth[[as.character(s)]]
  data.frame(scenario=s,sequence=keys,
    q=apply(doses,1,function(d)mean(p[cbind(d,1:J)])),
    safe=apply(doses,1,function(d)all(p[cbind(d,1:J)]<ei[2])),
    nonincreasing=nonincreasing,intensity=rowSums(doses))
}))
sequence_id <- paste(sequence_truth$scenario,sequence_truth$sequence,sep="/")
selected_id <- match(paste(trials$scenario,trials$selected_mts,sep="/"),sequence_id)
trials$recommend_safe <- FALSE
has_recommendation <- !is.na(selected_id)
trials$recommend_safe[has_recommendation] <- sequence_truth$safe[selected_id[has_recommendation]]
trials$recommend_unsafe <- trials$selected_mts!="None" & !trials$recommend_safe
trials$correct_safe <- trials$correct_selection & trials$true_mts!="None"
stopifnot(all(trials$selected_mts %in% c(candidate_keys,"None")))
cells$true_p <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(cells)),function(r) {
  truth[[as.character(cells$scenario[r])]][cells$dose[r],cells$cycle[r]]
},numeric(1))
cells$unsafe <- cells$true_p>=ei[2]

# Separate seeing the true sequence from choosing it once it has been seen.
# Completed-path records contain one row per completing patient, not per trial.
overview <- do.call(rbind,lapply(scenarios,function(s) {
  a <- subset(trials,scenario==s)
  p <- subset(completed,scenario==s)
  target_path <- true_mts[match(s,scenarios)]
  seen <- a$trial %in% p$trial[p$sequence==target_path]
  c <- subset(cells,scenario==s)
  qstar <- subset(sequence_truth,scenario==s & sequence==target_path)$q
  data.frame(scenario=s,true_mts=target_path,
    qstar=if(length(qstar))qstar else NA_real_,
    exact=mean(a$correct_selection),safe=mean(a$recommend_safe),
    unsafe=mean(a$recommend_unsafe),none=mean(a$selected_mts=="None"),
    stopped=mean(a$stopped_early),
    no_mts_without_stop=mean(a$selected_mts=="None" & !a$stopped_early),
    coverage=if(target_path=="None")NA_real_ else mean(seen),
    conditional_selection=if(any(seen))mean(a$correct_selection[seen]) else NA_real_,
    mean_true_path_patients=if(target_path=="None")NA_real_ else sum(p$sequence==target_path)/nrow(a),
    unsafe_exposure=sum(c$n[c$unsafe])/sum(c$n),
    mean_enrolled=mean(a$n_enrolled),mean_complete=mean(a$n_complete),
    mean_dlts=mean(a$dlts),mean_cycles=mean(a$patient_cycles))
}))
stopifnot(all(abs(overview$safe+overview$unsafe+overview$none-1)<1e-12))
with_oracle <- overview$true_mts!="None"
stopifnot(all(abs(overview$exact[with_oracle] -
  overview$coverage[with_oracle]*overview$conditional_selection[with_oracle])<1e-12))
stat <- function(s,name) overview[overview$scenario==s,name]
mean_cells <- aggregate(n~scenario+dose+cycle,cells,mean)
selection <- do.call(rbind,lapply(scenarios,function(s) {
  a <- subset(trials,scenario==s)
  labs <- c(candidate_keys,"None")
  data.frame(scenario=s,sequence=labs,
              probability=as.integer(table(factor(a$selected_mts,levels=labs)))/nrow(a))
}))
```

# What this exploration measures

We take the **current coded design as the fixed BaSyc benchmark**. This report
explores the saved `data/table3.rds`: `r nsim` trials in each of six scenarios,
`r nrow(trials)` trials total. It does not compare runs or try to match the
paper's numerical results. The copula section is a proposal only.

The saved run uses **strict n > 3** for intratrial safety and starts global
termination and exclusion after the first cohort completes its sequence.
Equal PAVA weights, higher-position nearest-target ties and the existing
restricted-revote fallback are retained. These recorded settings define this
benchmark throughout the exploration.

```{r recorded-settings}
show <- c("nsim_per_scenario","maximum_patients","cohort_size","cycles","target",
          "EI","safety_min_n","mts_screen_min_n","global_monitor",
          "pava_weights","nearest_tie","no_mts_fallback","outcome_generator","seed")
knitr::kable(saved$settings[match(show,saved$settings$setting),],row.names=FALSE,
             caption="Settings recorded in the input RDS")
```

Use three distinct questions to judge performance:

1. **Recommendation:** does the design choose the true MTS, another safe path,
   an unsafe path, or no path?
2. **Exploration:** does a patient ever complete the true MTS, so it can enter
   the final sequence-specific analysis?
3. **Patient allocation:** how much treatment is delivered in truly unsafe
   dose/cycle cells, and how many patients reach later cycles?

Here, a truly safe sequence has every cycle probability **below 0.35**, the
simulation's truth convention. This differs from the posterior safety event
used by the design, which compares an unknown cell probability with 0.30.
Exact-MTS selection is a stricter metric than selecting any safe sequence.
For S4 there is no safe sequence: **no recommendation is the correct decision**.
With 10,000 trials, the Monte Carlo standard error of an unconditional
probability is at most 0.5 percentage points. Conditional selection uses only
trials observing the true path and has a smaller effective denominator.

```{r operating-characteristics}
tab <- data.frame(Scenario=paste0("S",overview$scenario),
  True_MTS=short_sequence(overview$true_mts),
  Correct_decision_pct=100*overview$exact,
  Safe_recommendation_pct=100*overview$safe,
  Unsafe_recommendation_pct=100*overview$unsafe,
  No_MTS_pct=100*overview$none,Early_stop_pct=100*overview$stopped)
knitr::kable(tab,digits=2,row.names=FALSE,
  col.names=c("Scenario","True MTS","Correct decision (%)","Safe rec. (%)",
              "Unsafe rec. (%)","No MTS (%)","Early stop (%)"))
```

```{r recommendation-composition, fig.width=12, fig.height=5.3, fig.cap='Final recommendation categories, across all saved trials. In S4, the gray no-MTS category is the correct decision; the gold category refers only to a true safe MTS.'}
parts <- rbind(overview$exact,overview$safe-overview$exact,overview$unsafe,overview$none)
# S4 has no safe MTS: put all its correct decisions in the no-MTS category.
parts[1,overview$true_mts=="None"] <- 0
parts[2,overview$true_mts=="None"] <- 0
par(mar=c(4,4,3,1))
at <- barplot(100*parts,col=colors[c("correct","safe","unsafe","none")],
                border=NA,names.arg=paste0("S",scenarios),ylim=c(0,122),yaxt="n",
                ylab="Trials (%)",main="Final recommendations across the six scenarios")
axis(2,at=seq(0,100,20))
legend("top",c("True safe MTS","Other safe sequence","Unsafe sequence","No MTS"),
       fill=colors[c("correct","safe","unsafe","none")],ncol=2,bty="n",cex=.9)
for(s in seq_along(scenarios)) {
  centers <- cumsum(100*parts[,s])-50*parts[,s]
  show <- parts[,s]>=.075
  text(at[s],centers[show],sprintf("%.1f",100*parts[show,s]),cex=.9,
       col=ifelse(which(show)==4,"#253746","white"),font=2)
}
```

# Why the true scenarios differ

For a fixed three-cycle sequence, the truth criterion is

$$
q_s=\frac{p_{s_1,1}+p_{s_2,2}+p_{s_3,3}}{3},
\qquad \max_j p_{s_j,j}<0.35.
$$

The following plot shows all ten nonincreasing sequences. A TPC near 0.30
does not make a sequence safe when one cycle is overly toxic. Gold marks the
true MTS; red marks a sequence containing an unsafe cycle. The shaded region
is the EI, (0.25, 0.35).

```{r true-sequence-spectrum, fig.width=14, fig.height=9, fig.cap='True sequence TPC and cellwise safety. Blue and gold points are safe; red points contain an unsafe cycle. Gold identifies the true MTS. S5 and S6 use the highest safe sequence below target because no safe sequence reaches the EI.'}
op <- par(mfrow=c(2,3),mar=c(4,4.2,3,1),cex=.95)
for(s in scenarios) {
  a <- subset(sequence_truth,scenario==s)
  a <- a[match(candidate_keys,a$sequence),]
  y <- rev(seq_len(nrow(a)))
  limit <- min(1,max(.4,a$q)*1.12)
  plot(NA,xlim=c(0,limit),ylim=c(.4,nrow(a)+.6),xlab="True TPC",
       ylab="",yaxt="n",main=paste0("S",s," | true ",short_sequence(true_mts[s])))
  rect(ei[1],0,ei[2],nrow(a)+1,col="#EDF0F2",border=NA)
  abline(v=target,lty=2,col="#52636F")
  axis(2,at=y,labels=short_sequence(a$sequence),las=1,cex.axis=.9)
  is_true <- a$sequence==true_mts[s]
  points(a$q,y,pch=21,cex=ifelse(is_true,1.7,1.2),
         bg=ifelse(is_true,colors["correct"],ifelse(a$safe,colors["safe"],colors["unsafe"])))
}
par(op)
```

S1 and S2 have different cycle-specific safety frontiers despite similar
first-cycle probabilities. In S1, D2/C3 has probability 0.363 and is unsafe;
the true MTS is 221, with TPC 0.2705. In S2, D2/C3 is safe at 0.3267, making
222 the true MTS with TPC 0.2979. Its neighboring 221 has TPC **0.2495**,
just below the lower EI boundary. Small changes in the toxicity surface
therefore change which complete path the design must explore and recognize.

# Allocation and exposure

These plots use **all evaluated dose/cycle observations**, including those
from patients who did not finish three cycles and trials that stopped early.
They do not restrict allocation to patients completing nonincreasing paths.

## How much treatment reaches each cycle?

Each bar represents the `r N` planned patients in a trial. The gray portion
is the mean number without an evaluable observation in that cycle, combining
non-enrollment and failure to reach/complete that assessment. Thus later-cycle
bars retain the loss of follow-up rather than renormalizing the survivors to 100%.

```{r allocation-stacked, fig.width=14, fig.height=8.5, fig.cap='Mean evaluated patients per dose and cycle, per trial. Blue D1, green D2, purple D3; gray NA means no evaluated observation out of 15 planned patients. Numbers within sufficiently large segments identify dose and mean patient count.'}
op <- par(mfrow=c(2,3),mar=c(4,4,3,1),cex=.95)
for(s in scenarios) {
  m <- matrix(0,I,J)
  a <- subset(mean_cells,scenario==s)
  m[cbind(a$dose,a$cycle)] <- a$n
  values <- rbind(m,pmax(0,N-colSums(m)))
  at <- barplot(values,col=colors[c("D1","D2","D3","missing")],border="white",
                  names.arg=paste0("Cycle ",1:J),ylim=c(0,N+1),
                  ylab="Mean evaluated patients",main=paste("Scenario",s))
  for(j in 1:J) {
    center <- cumsum(values[,j])-values[,j]/2
    ok <- values[,j]>=1.1
    label <- ifelse(values[ok,j]>=2,
      paste0(c("D1","D2","D3","NA")[ok],"\n",sprintf("%.1f",values[ok,j])),
      paste0(c("D1","D2","D3","NA")[ok]," ",sprintf("%.1f",values[ok,j])))
    text(at[j],center[ok],label,cex=.8,
         col=ifelse(which(ok)==4,"#253746","white"),font=2)
  }
}
par(op)
```

## Which dose/cycle cells receive patients?

The heatmaps combine mean allocation with true toxicity. A red border marks
a truly unsafe cell; a gold inner border marks a cycle component of the true MTS.
Color intensity represents allocation on the same 0-to-15 scale in every panel.

```{r allocation-heatmap, fig.width=14, fig.height=8.5, fig.cap='Allocation heatmaps. Each cell gives mean evaluated patients n and true DLT probability p. Darker blue means more allocation; red borders mean p >= 0.35; gold borders locate the true MTS.'}
op <- par(mfrow=c(2,3),mar=c(4.5,4.5,3,1),mgp=c(2.8,.8,0),cex=.95)
palette <- colorRampPalette(c("#F5F9FC","#175C96"))(101)
for(s in scenarios) {
  p <- truth[[as.character(s)]]
  a <- subset(mean_cells,scenario==s)
  m <- matrix(0,I,J);m[cbind(a$dose,a$cycle)] <- a$n
  plot(NA,xlim=c(.5,J+.5),ylim=c(.5,I+.5),xlab="Cycle",ylab="Dose",
       xaxt="n",yaxt="n",main=paste("Scenario",s))
  axis(1,at=1:J);axis(2,at=1:I,labels=paste0("D",1:I),las=1)
  for(d in 1:I)for(j in 1:J) {
    rect(j-.48,d-.48,j+.48,d+.48,
         col=palette[1+round(100*m[d,j]/N)],border="white")
    if(p[d,j]>=ei[2])rect(j-.47,d-.47,j+.47,d+.47,border=colors["unsafe"],lwd=2)
    col <- if(m[d,j]>9)"white" else "#183849"
    text(j,d+.12,sprintf("n=%.2f",m[d,j]),cex=.9,col=col,font=2)
    text(j,d-.15,sprintf("p=%.3f",p[d,j]),cex=.85,col=col)
  }
  if(true_mts[s]!="None") {
    d <- as.integer(strsplit(true_mts[s],",",fixed=TRUE)[[1]])
    for(j in 1:J)rect(j-.40,d[j]-.40,j+.40,d[j]+.40,border=colors["correct"],lwd=3)
  }
}
par(op)
```

Define unsafe evaluated exposure using the truth, not the posterior decision:

$$
\text{Unsafe exposure}
=\frac{\sum_{b,d,j}n_{bdj}\,\mathbf1\{p_{dj}\ge0.35\}}
       {\sum_{b,d,j}n_{bdj}}.
$$

This is a patient-cycle proportion, not the percentage of distinct patients
ever receiving an unsafe dose. Multiple DLTs in one patient also contribute
multiple events to the mean DLT count.

```{r burden-table}
tab <- data.frame(Scenario=paste0("S",scenarios),
  Mean_enrolled=overview$mean_enrolled,Mean_complete=overview$mean_complete,
  Mean_evaluated_cycles=overview$mean_cycles,Mean_DLTs=overview$mean_dlts,
  Unsafe_exposure_pct=100*overview$unsafe_exposure)
knitr::kable(tab,digits=2,row.names=FALSE,
  col.names=c("Scenario","Mean enrolled","Mean completed","Mean evaluated cycles",
              "Mean DLTs","Unsafe exposure (%)"))
```

## How do doses move within patients?

The following diagram uses completed patient paths. Arrow width is
proportional to the mean number of patients following that transition per
trial; red arrows escalate, blue arrows de-escalate, and gray arrows stay.
Node labels give the mean number of completing patients at that dose/cycle.
This describes **completers only**; the preceding allocation plots include
all evaluated observations and should be used to assess exposure.

```{r allocation-transitions, fig.width=14, fig.height=8.5, fig.cap='Dose transitions among patients completing all three cycles. Nodes show mean completers per trial; widths show mean transition counts. Red means escalation, blue de-escalation and gray no change. Increasing paths are allowed during exploration even though the final recommendation is nonincreasing.'}
op <- par(mfrow=c(2,3),mar=c(4.5,4.5,3,1),mgp=c(2.8,.8,0),cex=.95)
for(s in scenarios) {
  a <- subset(completed,scenario==s)
  d <- do.call(rbind,strsplit(a$sequence,",",fixed=TRUE));storage.mode(d)<-"integer"
  plot(NA,xlim=c(.6,J+.4),ylim=c(.5,I+.5),xlab="Cycle",ylab="Dose",
       xaxt="n",yaxt="n",main=paste("Scenario",s))
  axis(1,at=1:J);axis(2,at=1:I,labels=paste0("D",1:I),las=1)
  for(j in 1:(J-1)) {
    flow <- table(factor(d[,j],levels=1:I),factor(d[,j+1],levels=1:I))/nsim
    for(from in 1:I)for(to in 1:I)if(flow[from,to]>.025) {
      col <- if(to>from)colors["unsafe"] else if(to<from)colors["safe"] else "#A3ADB5"
      arrows(j+.13,from,j+1-.13,to,col=adjustcolor(col,.75),
             lwd=.35+1.2*flow[from,to],length=.07,angle=20)
    }
  }
  for(j in 1:J)for(dose in 1:I) {
    rect(j-.13,dose-.16,j+.13,dose+.16,col="white",border="#4E6575",lwd=1.2)
    text(j,dose,sprintf("%.1f",sum(d[,j]==dose)/nsim),cex=.85)
  }
}
par(op)
```

# Exploration versus final selection

Let V be the event that at least one patient completes the true MTS.
Because final selection is restricted to observed completed sequences,

$$
\Pr(\widehat s=s^*)
=\Pr(V)\Pr(\widehat s=s^*\mid V).
$$

This identity separates a **coverage bottleneck** from selection after the
sequence has entered the dataset. The conditional quantity is descriptive:
trials visiting a path need not be comparable with those that do not.

```{r coverage-table}
tab <- subset(overview,true_mts!="None")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Scenario=paste0("S",tab$scenario),
  True_MTS=short_sequence(tab$true_mts),TPC=tab$qstar,
  Seen_pct=100*tab$coverage,Selected_pct=100*tab$exact,
  Selected_given_seen_pct=100*tab$conditional_selection,
  Mean_completers_on_true_MTS=tab$mean_true_path_patients),digits=2,row.names=FALSE,
  col.names=c("Scenario","True MTS","True TPC","Seen (%)","Selected (%)",
              "Selected given seen (%)","Mean patients on true MTS"))
```

```{r exploration-selection, fig.width=13, fig.height=5, fig.cap='True-MTS exploration and final selection. Left: probability of observing the true path at least once and of selecting it. Right: selection conditional on observing it. S4 has no safe MTS and is omitted.'}
a <- subset(overview,true_mts!="None")
op <- par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,4,3,1))
at <- barplot(100*rbind(a$coverage,a$exact),beside=TRUE,
       col=colors[c("safe","correct")],border=NA,
       names.arg=paste0("S",a$scenario),ylim=c(0,126),yaxt="n",
       ylab="Trials (%)",main="Did the trial observe the true sequence?")
axis(2,at=seq(0,100,20))
legend("top",c("Observed complete path","Selected true MTS"),
       fill=colors[c("safe","correct")],bty="n",cex=.9)
text(at[2,],100*a$exact,sprintf("%.1f",100*a$exact),pos=3,cex=.85)
at <- barplot(100*a$conditional_selection,col=colors["safe"],border=NA,
       names.arg=paste0("S",a$scenario),ylim=c(0,110),yaxt="n",
       ylab="Conditional selection (%)",main="If observed, was the true MTS selected?")
axis(2,at=seq(0,100,20))
text(at,100*a$conditional_selection,sprintf("%.1f",100*a$conditional_selection),pos=3,cex=.9)
par(op)
```

## What each scenario teaches

- **S1: a cycle-specific boundary.** The correct path is 221, with D2
  permissible in cycles 1 and 2 but unsafe in cycle 3. Coverage is
  `r percent(stat(1,"coverage"))`, and selection conditional on coverage is
  `r percent(stat(1,"conditional_selection"))`. Both exploration and final
  discrimination contribute. A pooled sequence TPC can also look acceptable
  while containing one unsafe cell.
- **S2: a rare complete optimal path.** The true 222 is observed in only
  `r percent(stat(2,"coverage"))` of trials. Conditional selection is
  `r percent(stat(2,"conditional_selection"))`, giving overall exact selection
  `r percent(stat(2,"exact"))`. Personal de-escalation and conservative
  cross-cycle allocation split patients onto other paths. The low exact
  selection rate therefore cannot be diagnosed from final PAVA alone.
- **S3: safe exploration is too slow to reach the upper boundary.** All dose/cycle
  cells are safe. The true 333 is observed in only `r percent(stat(3,"coverage"))`
  of trials, but selected in `r percent(stat(3,"conditional_selection"))` of
  trials observing it. With only five cohorts, an initial D1 cohort and
  conservative cross-cycle movement, this is predominantly a coverage limitation.
  Selecting 332 is underdosing relative to the exact oracle, not a toxicity failure.
- **S4: recognition and burden must both be measured.** There is no safe
  sequence. No MTS is returned in `r percent(stat(4,"none"))` of trials and
  global early termination occurs in `r percent(stat(4,"stopped"))`.
  The difference is no recommendation without a global early-stop flag.
  Nonetheless, mean exposure is `r sprintf("%.2f",stat(4,"mean_cycles"))`
  evaluated patient-cycles and `r sprintf("%.2f",stat(4,"mean_dlts"))` DLTs.
  Global monitoring begins after the first complete cohort sequence in this
  benchmark, so a high eventual stopping probability alone does not imply low burden.
- **S5: a large toxicity jump helps define the safe boundary.** D2 is safe,
  while D3 starts at 0.58. The true 222 has TPC 0.1765: no safe path reaches
  the EI, so the highest safe sequence below target is the oracle. Coverage is
  `r percent(stat(5,"coverage"))` and conditional selection is
  `r percent(stat(5,"conditional_selection"))`. This gives a clearer flat
  boundary than S1/S2, although unsafe recommendations still occur in
  `r percent(stat(5,"unsafe"))` of trials.
- **S6: the starting sequence is already optimal.** Only D1 is safe.
  The true 111 is always observed, so coverage is not the limitation.
  Exact and safe recommendation probabilities both equal
  `r percent(stat(6,"exact"))`. Unsafe alternatives such as 211 can have
  a TPC near target despite an unsafe first cycle. Moreover,
  `r percent(stat(6,"unsafe_exposure"))` of evaluated exposure is unsafe:
  its relatively high exact-selection probability should not obscure this burden.

These explanations combine the known truth geometry and observed allocations.
They are diagnostic interpretations, not causal effects established by
changing one design component at a time.

```{r final-selection-spectrum, fig.width=14, fig.height=10, fig.cap='Final selection by sequence. Gold is the true safe MTS, blue other safe sequences, red unsafe sequences, gray no MTS. Axes are percentages and panel limits vary to keep small probabilities readable; S4 no MTS is correct.'}
op <- par(mfrow=c(2,3),mar=c(4,4.2,3,1),cex=.95)
for(s in scenarios) {
  a <- subset(selection,scenario==s)
  q <- subset(sequence_truth,scenario==s)
  safe <- q$safe[match(a$sequence,q$sequence)];safe[is.na(safe)] <- FALSE
  col <- ifelse(a$sequence=="None",colors["none"],
           ifelse(a$sequence==true_mts[s],colors["correct"],
             ifelse(safe,colors["safe"],colors["unsafe"])))
  y <- rev(seq_len(nrow(a)));value <- 100*a$probability
  limit <- max(30,1.3*max(value))
  plot(NA,xlim=c(0,limit),ylim=c(.4,nrow(a)+.6),xaxt="n",yaxt="n",
       xlab="Trials selecting sequence (%)",ylab="",main=paste("Scenario",s))
  axis(1,at=seq(0,min(100,limit),by=if(limit<=40)10 else 20))
  axis(2,at=y,labels=short_sequence(a$sequence),las=1,cex.axis=.85)
  rect(0,y-.33,value,y+.33,col=col,border=NA)
  ok <- value>=1
  text(value[ok],y[ok],sprintf("%.1f",value[ok]),pos=4,cex=.8)
}
par(op)
```

# Copula stress tests: changing dependence between cycles

This section proposes a future experiment. **We change how a patient's
cycle outcomes are generated, while keeping the current coded design fixed.**
No copula generator or new stress-test simulation is run by this notebook.

We explain one scenario and one patient at a time. The scenario and trial
replicate labels are omitted from the equations; each patient receives a
fresh set of random numbers when the experiment is eventually run.

## What assumption changes from the original simulation?

Let $p_{dj}$ be the specified DLT probability for **dose $d$ in cycle $j$**.
These are the same six dose/cycle probability surfaces used above. In the
original generator, a patient's outcome in one cycle gives no information
about the random number generating that patient's next outcome. The copula
proposal replaces that **within-patient independence** with positive association.

Here, independence refers to the **unobserved cycle-specific random numbers**.
Even in the original adaptive trial, observed DLTs need not be independent:
an earlier DLT can change the next dose. The copula adds association beyond
that dose-decision pathway.

| Part of the experiment | Original generator | Copula generator |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Fixed-dose risk $p_{dj}$ | Saved dose/cycle probabilities | Same probabilities |
| Association across one patient's cycles | Independent random numbers | Associated random numbers |
| Association between different patients | Independent patient vectors | Independent patient vectors |
| Dose monotonicity within a cycle | Same random number thresholds all candidate doses | Same construction |
| Allocation, monitoring and recommendation | Current coded rules | Same rules |
| Fixed-sequence TPC, safety and true MTS | Determined by the saved $p_{dj}$ | Same marginal definitions and labels |

The design receives observed doses and DLTs. It does not receive a copula
parameter. Its beta-binomial working calculations and decision rules are
retained, although their operating characteristics can change when the
outcome generator changes. In particular, retaining the algorithm does not
guarantee its working assumptions describe the new data exactly.

Keep the recorded strict $n>3$ safety convention, global-monitoring and
exclusion timing, equal PAVA weights, higher-position ties, final screening
and restricted-revote fallback. The target remains 0.30, the EI is
(0.25, 0.35), and the posterior safety cutoff is 0.95. The pending
target-dependent PAVA tie hypothesis belongs to a later design comparison.

## How uniform random numbers become DLT outcomes

For this patient, let $U_j$ be an unobserved random number between zero and
one for cycle $j$. Each $U_j$ is uniformly distributed. If the patient were
given dose $d$ in that cycle, define the potential outcome

$$
Y_{dj}=\mathbf1\{U_j\le p_{dj}\}.
$$

Here $Y_{dj}=1$ means a DLT and $Y_{dj}=0$ means no DLT. For example, a dose
with risk 0.20 causes a DLT whenever $U_j\le0.20$. Uniformity gives
$\Pr(Y_{dj}=1)=p_{dj}$.

Use the same $U_j$ for all candidate doses in that cycle. Increasing the
dose can then change no DLT to DLT, but cannot change DLT to no DLT when
$p_{dj}$ increases with dose. This threshold coupling is already present
in the original generator; it is not the new dependence assumption.

Write $D_j$ for the dose actually assigned in cycle $j$. Only
$Y_{D_j,j}$ is revealed, at its scheduled assessment. Other potential
outcomes and future outcomes stay hidden from the trial rules.

A **copula** describes how the three uniform random numbers go together:

$$
C(u_1,u_2,u_3)
=\Pr(U_1\le u_1,\ U_2\le u_2,\ U_3\le u_3).
$$

The arguments $u_1,u_2,u_3$ are cutoffs, not doses or extra parameters.
For any copula, $C(u,1,1)=u$, and likewise for the other cycles. Thus it
can change joint probabilities while keeping each individual risk fixed.
The original independence copula is simply

$$
C(u_1,u_2,u_3)=u_1u_2u_3.
$$

For a fixed sequence $(d_1,d_2,d_3)$, the probability of three DLTs is
$C(p_{d_1,1},p_{d_2,2},p_{d_3,3})$. The independent generator gives the
product of those three risks. The next two families replace that product
with different patterns of positive association.

## Gaussian copula: a shared patient component, controlled by rho

The Gaussian copula starts with three correlated normal scores and turns
them into uniform random numbers. A convenient construction is

$$
Z_j=\sqrt{\rho}\,B+\sqrt{1-\rho}\,\varepsilon_j,
\qquad U_j=\Phi(Z_j),
\qquad j=1,2,3.
$$

The patient has one shared score $B$. Each cycle has its own score
$\varepsilon_j$. All four input scores are independent standard normals
(mean zero, variance one). $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative
distribution function: it converts a normal score into its percentile.
Consequently, each $U_j$ is uniform.

**What does $\rho$ mean?** It is the correlation between any two normal
scores $Z_j$, not between the observed binary DLT outcomes. It is also the
fraction of each score's variance supplied by the shared component. At
$\rho=0$ there is no shared contribution and the cycles are independent.
At $\rho=0.5$, half the variance is shared and half is cycle-specific.
As $\rho$ approaches one, the three scores increasingly move together.

A patient with a low shared score tends to have low uniforms in several
cycles, making repeated DLTs more likely. These scores are mathematical
simulation devices, not measured biomarkers or PK/PD parameters.

The formal copula CDF is

$$
C_G(u_1,u_2,u_3;\rho)
=\Phi_3\!\left(\Phi^{-1}(u_1),\Phi^{-1}(u_2),\Phi^{-1}(u_3);R_\rho\right),
$$

$$
R_\rho=\begin{pmatrix}
1&\rho&\rho\\
\rho&1&\rho\\
\rho&\rho&1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Here $\Phi^{-1}$ converts a percentile back to a normal score, and
$\Phi_3$ computes the joint probability for three normal scores.
The matrix says that each score has variance one and every cycle pair
has correlation $\rho$. We propose $0\le\rho<1$: **one parameter for all
three pairs**, including cycles 1 and 3. There is no separate lag parameter.

## Clayton copula: clustering of small uniforms, controlled by theta

For positive association, the three-cycle Clayton copula is

$$
C_C(u_1,u_2,u_3;\theta)
=\left(u_1^{-\theta}+u_2^{-\theta}+u_3^{-\theta}-2\right)^{-1/\theta},
\qquad \theta>0.
$$

**What does $\theta$ mean?** It controls the strength of association.
Larger values give stronger association; independence is the limit as
$\theta$ approaches zero. It is not a probability or a binary correlation.
The same parameter governs all cycle pairs.

The formula preserves the uniform margins. For example,

$$
C_C(u,1,1;\theta)
=\left(u^{-\theta}+1+1-2\right)^{-1/\theta}=u.
$$

The minus two cancels the contributions from the other two cycles when
their cutoffs are one. At a zero cutoff the joint CDF is zero by continuity.
At $\theta=0$, use the independent-uniform branch directly rather than
substituting zero into a formula containing $1/\theta$.

One way to generate these uniforms also uses a shared patient component:

$$
\begin{aligned}
W&\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\text{shape}=1/\theta,\text{rate}=1),\\
E_1,E_2,E_3&\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Exp}(\text{rate}=1).
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
U_j=\left(1+\frac{E_j}{W}\right)^{-1/\theta}.
$$

$W$ is a positive random number shared by the patient's cycles; the
$E_j$ are independent positive numbers giving cycle-specific variation,
also independent of $W$. For a fixed $\theta$, a small $W$ pushes several
uniforms toward zero. Since our DLT rule uses small uniforms, this produces
clustering of toxicities. The gamma and exponential draws are a sampling
recipe; **$\theta$ is still the only free dependence parameter**.

This concentration near jointly small uniforms is called **lower-tail
dependence**. Gaussian association is symmetric between low and high
uniform ranks; Clayton emphasizes the low end. A Gaussian copula can also
produce repeated DLTs at clinical thresholds. Neither construction adds
a causal effect of the previous dose to $p_{dj}$: statistical association
between cycles and pharmacologic carryover are different assumptions.

## Comparing the two parameters on a common scale

A Gaussian $\rho$ of 0.5 and a Clayton $\theta$ of 0.5 do not represent the
same association. We therefore choose **Kendall's tau**, written $\tau$,
first and convert it to each family's parameter.

To understand tau, compare two independent patients' uniforms in two
cycles. Their rankings agree if the patient with the smaller uniform in
one cycle also has the smaller uniform in the other cycle. Tau is the
probability of agreeing rankings minus the probability of reversed
rankings. It is zero at independence for these families and approaches
one as the ranks move together. It refers to the **unobserved uniforms**;
$\tau=0.4$ does not mean a 40% binary DLT correlation or a 40% chance of
repeated toxicity.

The conversions are

$$
\tau=\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin(\rho)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\rho=\sin(\pi\tau/2)
\qquad\text{(Gaussian)},
$$

$$
\tau=\frac{\theta}{\theta+2}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\theta=\frac{2\tau}{1-\tau}
\qquad\text{(Clayton)}.
$$

| Chosen latent $\tau$ | Gaussian $\rho$ | Clayton $\theta$ | Meaning in this experiment |
|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| 0 | 0 | 0, using the independence branch | Original independent generator |
| 0.2 | 0.3090 | 0.5000 | Weaker positive association |
| 0.4 | 0.5878 | 1.3333 | Intermediate positive association |
| 0.6 | 0.8090 | 3.0000 | Stronger positive association |

Tau is a way of specifying the same single parameter, not an additional
parameter to estimate. These settings cover positive association only.
Matching tau matches rank association for all three cycle pairs. It does
not match binary DLT correlations, all three-cycle probabilities, or the
entire joint distribution. A Gaussian-versus-Clayton contrast therefore
compares distributional shapes at matched tau, not a pure tail effect.

## What stays fixed, and what can change for a patient?

For a fixed sequence $(d_1,d_2,d_3)$, let $K$ be the number of DLTs over
its three complete cycles. Regardless of the copula,

$$
E(K)=p_{d_1,1}+p_{d_2,2}+p_{d_3,3},
\qquad
q(d_1,d_2,d_3)=\frac{E(K)}3.
$$

Thus the mean TPC is unchanged. The saved safety definition still requires
every cycle risk to be below 0.35, so the marginal true MTS is unchanged
and S4 still has no safe MTS. The copula changes how DLTs are distributed
among patients and cycles, including the probabilities of any or repeated
DLTs. It is not a new definition of the optimal sequence.

For transparent arithmetic only, suppose all three fixed-cycle risks are
0.20. With Clayton $\theta=1$, the probability of three DLTs is

$$
C_C(0.20,0.20,0.20;1)=\frac1{5+5+5-2}=\frac1{13}.
$$

The following values are exact calculations, not simulated results or an
additional planned scenario:

| Generator in this illustration | $E(K)$ | At least one DLT | At least two DLTs | Three DLTs |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Independent cycles | 0.600 | 0.488 | 0.104 | 0.008 |
| Clayton, $\theta=1$ | 0.600 | 0.344 | 0.179 | 0.077 |

The average burden is identical, but the Clayton example has more
DLT-free patients and more patients with repeated DLTs. For other unequal
risks, calculate the joint event probabilities rather than assuming every
multiple-DLT metric changes in the same direction.

## Why can allocation performance change if the rules stay the same?

The rules do not use a copula parameter, but they **react to earlier DLTs**.
With positive association, an earlier DLT gives information about the
patient's later outcomes even before the next dose is chosen.

Continue the fixed-risk 0.20 example with Clayton $\theta=1$. The chance
of DLT in both cycles 1 and 2 is

$$
C_C(0.20,0.20,1;1)=\frac19.
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(\text{DLT in cycle 2}\mid\text{DLT in cycle 1})
&=\frac{1/9}{0.20}=\frac59\approx0.556,\\
\Pr(\text{DLT in cycle 2}\mid\text{no DLT in cycle 1})
&=\frac{0.20-1/9}{0.80}=\frac19\approx0.111.
\end{aligned}
$$

These conditional probabilities average back to 0.20. Under the original
independent generator, both would be 0.20. The example uses fixed doses;
in BaSyc the prior outcome also changes the next dose. De-escalated
patients can therefore be enriched for susceptibility, while escalating
patients can be selected for tolerance.

This distinguishes a **fixed-dose marginal risk** from the risk among
patients actually assigned to that cell:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(Y_{dj}=1)&=p_{dj},\\
\Pr(Y_{dj}=1\mid D_j=d,\ \text{earlier observed history})
&\ \text{may differ from }p_{dj}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The first probability remains fixed in the copula experiment. The second
equals that margin in the original independent construction, but need not
do so under dependence. Later-cycle empirical cell rates can therefore
shift even when the copula generator has correct fixed-dose margins.
There is no guarantee that dependence always increases early stopping
or unsafe recommendations.

Cycle 1 is a useful control: a new patient's vector is independent of
previous patients, and the first dose is chosen before that patient's own
outcomes are known. Its assigned-cell risk should still agree with $p_{d1}$.
History-specific summaries should record any previous DLT and the previous
dose, with full histories retained for review.

## How the proposed experiment would be carried out

The parameters are known simulation inputs. They are not estimated from
an individual 15-patient trial. Use all six saved surfaces and the common
tau grid above: one independence setting and six dependent settings per
scenario, or **42 conditions**. At 10,000 trials per condition this means
420,000 trial replicates, including 60,000 independent baseline trials;
the nonzero-dependence conditions require 360,000 new trial replicates.
This remains a proposal, not a request to launch those runs now.

1. **Freeze the benchmark.** Use the current saved settings, marginal risks,
   safety definition and true MTS. Keep the pending PAVA tie change and any
   new safety/fallback rule outside this first dependence comparison.

2. **Use the same base random numbers across conditions.** Retain the
   original 15-by-3 independent-uniform bank and its draw order for each
   trial. Draw one extra shared number per patient after that bank, or from
   a documented auxiliary stream. Different trial replicates use independent
   banks; reuse each trial's bank across the compared conditions. Transform
   these numbers using the
   Gaussian or Clayton construction. At tau zero, return the original
   uniforms directly and reproduce every saved trial, cell and completed
   path record before reusing the existing baseline. **Do not redraw a
   fresh independent number after an intrapatient dose decision.**

3. **Validate the generator before running a trial design.** Plan 200,000
   independent latent patients for each of the seven settings, applying
   all six surfaces and all 27 fixed sequences. Check uniform margins,
   latent tau, the dose monotonicity of potential outcomes, fixed-dose DLT
   rates, pairwise and three-cycle probabilities, and the distribution of
   the full-cycle count $K$. Use the copula CDF for analytic joint targets
   and inclusion-exclusion for any/multiple-DLT probabilities. Account for
   Monte Carlo uncertainty across the collection of checks, record normal
   CDF tolerances, and require exact behavior when a risk is zero or one.

4. **Reveal outcomes in the usual trial order.** Give each potential patient
   one pre-generated vector. Assign doses using observed history only;
   reveal only outcomes at assigned doses when follow-up is due. Apply the
   unchanged counting, DCR, exclusion and global-monitoring order, then the
   unchanged recommendation and fallback. Save data before rendering.

5. **Retain decision, exposure and patient-burden outcomes.** Record exact
   MTS selection; safe, unsafe and no recommendation; coverage and selection
   given coverage; unsafe exposure; enrollment, completion and evaluated
   cycles; and observed any/multiple DLTs. Retain the first stop's time,
   triggering cycle, numerator, denominator, posterior risk and monitoring
   activation time, plus fallback use and patient dose/outcome histories.
   Keep unobserved cycles missing. Interpret observed DLT counts alongside
   follow-up length and keep them separate from full fixed-sequence counts.

6. **Compare paired trial results with uncertainty.** Compare each condition
   with independence and compare the families at matching tau. Because
   conditions reuse base patients, use the standard deviation of paired
   trial differences divided by the square root of the trial count for
   mean differences. For ratios, conditional quantities and history strata,
   resample whole paired trials. Report 95% Monte Carlo intervals, counts
   for sparse groups, and all prespecified conditions. A single probability
   from 10,000 trials has MCSE at most 0.5 percentage points; other metrics
   have their own uncertainty.

For each dose/cycle, also compare the observed DLT fraction with $p_{dj}$.
At independence, its difference should be compatible with zero; under
dependence, later-cycle departures can reflect selection by history.
Generator validation and the cycle-1 control help distinguish that mechanism
from a coding error.

Read the results through the questions in Sections 1--4: did the design
fail to explore the true path, fail to recognize it after exploring it,
or deliver an undesirable toxicity burden despite selecting it? Plot those
metrics and global stopping against tau, together with stopping time,
exposure and patient burden. A stable recommendation rate alone does not
establish robustness. This experiment evaluates the current design under
chosen dependence models; it does not identify the generator used in the
paper. A future objective based on repeated toxicity, rather than marginal
TPC, would need its own dependence-specific true optimum.


# References

- [Lyu, Curran and Ji (2018), BaSyc](https://doi.org/10.1200/PO.18.00020):
  source of the dose/cycle design and the marginal simulation scenarios.
  The benchmark here is the current coded version with its recorded conventions.
- [Hofert, Kojadinovic, Maechler and Yan, *Elements of Copula Modeling with R*, Chapter 2](https://copula.r-forge.r-project.org/book/02_copulas.html):
  Gaussian/Clayton constructions, Kendall-tau relationships and tail coefficients.
- [Marshall and Olkin (1988), *Families of Multivariate Distributions*](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1988.10478671):
  mixture-based construction underlying the shared-frailty sampling approach.
- [The `copula` package's Clayton implementation](https://github.com/cran/copula/blob/master/R/claytonCopula.R):
  explicit gamma-frailty generation with shape $1/\theta$ and rate one,
  including an independence branch.
- [Cunanan and Koopmeiners (2014), copula misspecification in Phase I--II trials](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4234400/):
  precedent for separating a data-generating association model from a fitted
  working model. Its efficacy/toxicity setting differs from this repeated-cycle
  experiment; the present protocol makes its own robustness assessment.
